Painted in May 1890, the artwork is coveted not only for its aesthetic beauty but for the late chapter of van Gogh’s tumultuous life when it was created. After spending a year in a psychiatric asylum following a mental health crisis during which he cut off his ear, the painter traveled to the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, near Paris. There, van Gogh became inspired by what he described as “beautiful greenery in abundance” and felt that “the desire to work will devour me and make me insensible to everything else and in a good mood,” according to a statement from Sotheby’s, the auction house hosting the painting’s sale.
But just two months into van Gogh’s stay in Auvers-sur-Oise, the painter shot himself in the chest. He succumbed to his injury two days later on July 29, 1890, at 37 years old.

“Ah well, I risk my life for my own work and my reason has half foundered in it,” van Gogh wrote in an unfinished letter addressed to his brother, Theo, which he was carrying with him on the day of the shooting. “But what can you do?”

Chestnut Trees in Blossom, which features a row of blooming trees and a man who resembles van Gogh walking by a trio of women, passed into Theo’s hands following the painter’s death. It was later owned by Theo’s widow, then the couple’s son, before if left the family.

Since 1975, the painting has been owned by the late Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, Argentine art collectors and patrons. Sotheby’s has titled the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection, simply, “Legendary.”

Joining Chestnut Trees in Blossom in the Blaquier-Arrieta sale are works by Impressionist masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Camille Pissarro. The entire auction, which opens on November 18, is expected to generate $450 million in sales.

“What strikes me most is that the Blaquier-Arrieta collection doesn’t feel like a private collection at all. It feels like a small museum—a miniature Musée d’Orsay, now opening its doors for the very first time,” Simon Shaw, a senior adviser at Sotheby’s, says in the statement.

Chestnut Trees in Blossom is one of just eight landscapes van Gogh created in Auvers-sur-Oise that remains in private hands. Its enthusiastic reception in Hong Kong lead Niichel to speculate that “Asia is certainly a possibility” for where the painting will wind up, per the Agence France-Presse.

“I’d never heard of this painting before, so I wanted to see it with my own eyes,” Li Shanshan, an art lover who traveled two and half hours from Shenzhen to view the piece in Hong Kong, tells the BBC. “I think it will create a huge sensation around the world.”

In a new study, the researchers found that movement-induced chronic back pain was tied to increased activity in the brain's default mode network, a group of connected brain regions that lights up during self-reflection and mind wandering. This finding was unexpected because the network typically becomes less active during acute pain, such as transient pain triggered from touching a hot stove or banging your knee on a table.
The new study, published Oct. 5 in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, suggests that chronic-pain flare-ups may involve brain processes beyond those responsible for detecting painful sensations.

Chronic lower back pain, defined as lasting at least three months, is a leading cause of disability worldwide. It's thought that when chronic pain first begins, a network of regions in the brain called the "pain neuromatrix" becomes sensitized so that the pain persists even after the painful stimulus is gone. Although scientists know that chronic pain is associated with changes in brain activity, they don't fully understand what happens when movements trigger sudden increases in that ongoing pain.

To investigate, researchers recruited 114 adults with chronic lower back pain and used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine their brain activity. fMRI measures changes in blood flow, which acts as an indirect measure of brain activity.

After an initial scan, a researcher helped lift each participant's leg until their back pain increased, held it in position for 10 seconds, and then lowered it. The researchers scanned the participants' brains immediately after this pain-inducing leg movement and compared the results with scans collected beforehand. On average, the test increased the participants' reported pain intensity by 23%.

As expected, during the leg movement, the researchers observed increased blood flow in brain regions involved in processing pain and movement. But they also detected increased activity in key regions of the default mode network, which typically becomes more active when a person is thinking about themselves or their autobiographical memories or just letting their mind wander.

"When we saw just the first round of analysis, we're like, 'Did we do it right?'" study co-author Morgan Gianola, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of California, San Diego, told Live Science.

"We did not expect [the default mode network] to be involved at all," said study co-author Fadel Zeidan, a neuroscientist at UC San Diego, told Live Science. "We expected it to be deactivated to the point that we had to triple-check our work to make sure that the results were legit."

The researchers also exposed participants' calves to painful heat — a common method of studying brain activity during acute pain. Unlike the movement-induced back pain, the heat was associated with reduced activity in part of the default mode network, suggesting a different mechanism was at play.
When pain becomes part of our internal experience

Participants who reported more severe chronic back pain had stronger connectivity between the default mode network and brain regions that process sensations from the back. This suggests that chronic pain may become intertwined with how people perceive themselves and their bodies, the study authors concluded.
"This pain flare has almost become a part of who they are from an egocentric perspective," Zeidan said.

Katherine Martucci, a neuroscientist at Duke University who wasn't involved in the study, praised the experimental design, noting that researchers typically avoid movement during brain scans because it can interfere with the clarity of the scan. This study "nicely gets around" that problem by taking scans before and after the painful motion, Martucci told Live Science in an email.

However, she noted that the observed brain activity could also reflect lingering pain or anxiety following the painful leg raise. In addition, the study couldn't determine whether the altered brain activity observed contributes to chronic pain or develops in response to it.

Nonetheless, Zeidan and colleagues think the findings could eventually inform future treatments for chronic pain. The therapies might address how people relate to their pain, rather than solely targeting the painful sensations themselves. Zeidan, who coincidentally developed chronic back pain while conducting the study, believes that people's past experiences and memories with chronic pain have influenced their brain processes to a point where the pain itself becomes part of who they are.

Zeidan's team is now investigating whether existing approaches, such as mindfulness meditation or cognitive behavioral therapy, can influence the default mode network and help relieve chronic pain. (Cognitive behavior therapy for chronic pain, or CBT-CP, is already a well-established treatment option.)

Martucci cautioned that it's too early to draw conclusions about how these results might be applied in clinical practice. But she said the current findings provide important evidence of how the brain responds to chronic pain flare-ups.

"They do provide solid data on how people with chronic low back pain show important changes in their brain responses after a condition provoking their pain," she said. "The brain imaging data validate their [the participants'] experience of pain in an important and very visible way."

Ancient DNA from skeletons buried in a historic cemetery in Quebec is changing people's understanding of their Indigenous ancestry. Contrary to popular belief, there may be little truth to stories of intermarriage between Indigenous and French people during the early days of colonization, according to a new archaeology study published Oct. 5 in the journal PNAS.

"Family stories of an Indigenous ancestor are very common" in Quebec, study first author Diane Martin-Moya, a biological anthropologist at the University of Quebec in Trois-Rivières in Canada, told Live Science in an email, and "commercial genealogy and DNA tests have amplified this." But distant or claimed Indigenous identities can actually undermine the rights, resources and recognition of Indigenous nations, she said.

To learn more about the founders of Quebec, Martin-Moya and co-authors investigated Notre-Dame Cemetery, which was established in Montreal in 1683 and used for Catholic burials until 1796. Based on previous studies of the skeletons in the cemetery, experts disagreed on whether people of Indigenous, European, African or mixed ancestry were buried there. To settle the question, Martin-Moya and her colleagues sequenced DNA from 45 people buried in the cemetery and compared it with the genomes of people from Europe, West Africa and Indigenous groups in the Americas.

"The ancient DNA showed that all 45 individuals we analyzed had French European ancestry, with no sign of recent Indigenous or African admixture," Martin-Moya said of the research, which she conducted while at the University of Montreal.

These findings suggest that people descended from Indigenous and African populations may have been marginalized in early Montreal, challenging the popular narrative of cooperation and intermarriage, she said.

"Our sample is small and comes from a single cemetery, so this does not show that such unions never happened," Martin-Moya cautioned. "It is, however, consistent with genealogical and genetic studies suggesting that Indigenous ancestry among present-day French Canadians is very limited."

The apparent lack of genetic mixing among European, African and Indigenous populations in this cemetery group "provides a perspective on population relationships during the colonial period, one where perhaps nongenetic interactions were present but no biological relationships were found," Raquel Fleskes, a molecular anthropologist at Dartmouth College who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

The DNA helped the researchers find several genetic lineages of people that spanned multiple generations. But the graves were scattered across multiple areas of the cemetery, suggesting that burials were not organized into family plots. This finding suggests that, in the 17th century, people in Montreal may have been burying their dead in a way that was not defined by strict biological kinship ties, Fleskes said.
Martin-Moya stressed that the results of the new study do not necessarily apply to all of colonial Montreal.
"Not identifying recent Indigenous or African admixture in this sample does not imply that Indigenous or African-descended people were absent from the city," Martin-Moya said.
In addition, "biological ancestry cannot by itself establish Indigenous belonging," as it "is rooted in kinship, community and relationships with land, not in blood or DNA," she added.
Changes in the use of the cemetery over time also may have influenced the findings, as reburials and later urban development disturbed or destroyed earlier graves.

"Those buried inside the church, mostly clergy and wealthier residents, were more likely to be exhumed and moved," Martin-Moya explained, while the city's poorer residents were buried outside the church and further buried beneath the expanding city. This means that the skeletons in the study may have been the remains of lower-class French colonists.

Archival records show that some Indigenous people were buried in Catholic cemeteries in Montreal as early as the 17th century, Martin-Moya said. "Over time, though, Indigenous communities were increasingly separated from the colonial town through land dispossession and the relocation of missions away from urban centers," she explained. "Their dead would most likely have been buried in those communities. Enslaved people, both Indigenous and African, were often buried on their enslaver's property or in cemeteries for the poor."

The results of the study don't mean that Québécois have no Indigenous ancestors or that relations between French settlers and Indigenous peoples were only hostile, Martin-Moya said. Those relationships were complex and included alliances, trade, conflict and, sometimes, family ties.

"What our results suggest is that when such ancestry exists, it needs to be put in context," Martin-Moya said. "A single ancestor who lived more than 300 years ago does not say the same thing about a person today as being raised within an Indigenous family, community or nation."

A modified tapeworm medication could be a promising new treatment for endometriosis, an early study in mice hints.

In endometriosis, tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside the organ, and these patches of tissue, called "lesions," trigger painful inflammation and heavy menstrual bleeding. In the new study, scientists fitted an anti-worm drug with nanotech armor, and it directly targeted these painful lesions in laboratory mice.

The treatment reduced inflammation and slowed or prevented further spread of the lesions, researchers reported in August in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials. The team is already working on bringing the new drug to clinical trials and hopes this will bring fresh attention to an understudied disease with limited treatment options.
Rogue immune cells are a promising drug target

Endometriosis is a chronic, hormone-driven condition that affects roughly 10% of reproductive-age females — an estimated 190 million individuals worldwide. "The main symptoms are chronic pelvic pain and infertility," said Ioannis Simitsidellis, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Edinburgh's Centres for Reproductive Health and Inflammation Research, who wasn't involved in the study.

There is currently no cure, so existing treatments aim to alleviate the symptoms. Hormonal medications can stall the menstrual cycle to limit the growth and inflammation of the lesions, while surgery can physically remove lesions. However, the former can come with side effects, such as nausea and mood swings, and lesions often regrow after surgery. So additional options are needed.

In previous research with mice, study co-author Kanako Hayashi, a professor in the Washington State University School of Molecular Biosciences, identified a group of rogue immune cells specific to endometrial lesion tissue. These cells turbocharged the painful inflammatory reactions and drove the growth of more of this problematic tissue.

The cells also happen to have a unique chemical label, called a folate receptor, which makes them an excellent potential drug target. But why start from scratch when there's an existing medication that might do the trick?

Enter niclosamide, a drug approved by the Food and Drug Administration to treat tapeworm infections. In recent years, clinicians have been exploring whether this medicine could also prove effective for other conditions, ranging from cancer to Parkinson's disease.

"We have reported that niclosamide inhibits endometriosis progression, suppressing the inflammatory mechanisms and cytokine secretions," said Hayashi, referencing more of the group's past work in mice. However, several issues made the drug impractical: It doesn't dissolve well in water, last long in the body, or target the cells where it's needed most.

So the researchers teamed up with Anjali Sharma, a nanomedicine specialist at the University of Michigan, to tweak the drug's structure. Using click chemistry — a simple reaction that bolts together two chemical building blocks — Sharma attached the niclosamide unit to a large, tree-like molecule called a dendrimer. This helped the drug dissolve better in blood.
She then added a folate group, which ensured that the modified medication would only target the rogue immune cells with the complementary receptor.

"The drug is attached in such a way that when it is in systemic circulation, nothing happens until it goes inside the diseased cells," Sharma said. Once there, it is slowly released inside the cell over a period of two weeks. "Basically, the dendrimer is like the Uber, the folate is like the GPS, and the drug is like the passenger," she explained.

With these practical issues resolved, the team tested the modified drug in a mouse model, which mimics the lesions seen in endometriosis in humans. Scans of the mice showed that the treatment directly zeroed in on the affected endometrial tissue and didn't accumulate in other organs, like the liver.
Treating mice with a single injection dramatically reduced their pain symptoms, compared with untreated mice. It also slowed — or, in some cases, entirely halted — the growth of new lesions.

Because mice don't naturally menstruate or develop endometriosis, there is still significant work to do before these findings can be replicated in humans. But for now, the study is a promising stepping stone for future research, Simitsidellis said.

"There's a lot of potential in repurposing of drugs that have been tested in clinical trials to see if they would be effective in endometriosis — for example, targeting inflammation or immune cell dysfunction," he told Live Science. "The next steps would be to replicate on larger sample sizes and, if that's promising, do a phase one clinical trial in humans." That initial trial would test the treatment's safety in patients, while later trials would look at its effectiveness for endometriosis.
Even at this early stage, though, patients are clamoring to get involved in the upcoming research. Hayashi and Sharma have received hundreds of emails asking to join a future trial.
"They are really suffering," Hayashi said. "Endometriosis is an understudied, underacknowledged, underfunded disease, but hopefully we can make this a solution in the near future."

The Audi valvelift system, or AVS, is a two-stage variable-valve-lift system. Instead of changing only a camshaft’s angular position, AVS changes the lobe that operates the intake, exhaust or both valves. A small or short-duration profile reduces pumping losses at partial load; while a larger profile improves cylinder filling or exhaust flow under load. Some versions add a zero-lift profile for cylinder deactivation.

AVS first appeared globally on Audi’s 2.8-liter FSI V6 and reached North America on the 3.2-liter FSI V6 for 2008. Audi subsequently used it on some 2.0 TFSI EA888 four-cylinders; the 2.5 TFSI EA855 evo; 2.9- and turbocharged 3.0-liter EA839 V6 engines; 4.0 TFSI V8s; the second-generation 5.2 FSI V10; and the 6.3 FSI W12. European applications include the 1.4 TFSI cylinder-on-demand engine and 4.0 TDI V8. The supercharged EA837 3.0 TFSI is an important exception: Audi states that it does not use AVS.

Volkswagen-brand applications include the intake-side system on the EA888 Generation III B 2.0 TSI introduced in the 2018 Tiguan and related B-cycle applications. European 1.4- and 1.5-liter TSI engines use the sliding-cam principle for Active Cylinder Technology, or ACT. Equipment varies by output, market and engine code, so never identify AVS by displacement or badge alone.

AVS can be installed on either side. The longitudinal Audi EA888 2.0 TFSI originally used AVS on its single exhaust camshaft. Volkswagen’s EA888 Generation III B uses it on the intake camshaft. A V6 may have it on one intake camshaft per bank, or two camshafts. Cylinder-deactivation V8 and V10 versions switch both intake and exhaust valves on the affected cylinders, sealing them with all valves closed.

The basic camshaft carries external splines. Cylindrical cam pieces, sometimes called cam sleeves, fit over those splines and carry two or more adjacent lobe profiles. Electromagnetic actuators are mounted in the cam cover or camshaft frame above the sleeves.

When the ECM commands a change, it briefly energizes an actuator and extends a metal pin into a helical groove in the rotating cam piece. The groove converts rotation into axial movement, sliding the sleeve until the alternate lobe aligns with the follower. A spring-loaded detent holds the sleeve, and a return ramp pushes the actuator pin back, inducing a voltage pulse that confirms the shift. A second actuator and groove move the sleeve in the opposite direction.

AVS and variable valve timing are separate systems. AVS changes lift and duration by selecting lobes. A hydraulic camshaft adjuster rotates the entire camshaft relative to the crankshaft, changing when the valves open and close. The ECM coordinates both with throttle angle, load, speed, boost and temperature.

On an intake-side B-cycle engine, the small profile provides a shorter opening period and earlier closing point. Cam phasing positions that event. Under higher load, AVS selects the longer profile and the phaser moves toward an Otto-cycle strategy. Exhaust-side systems coordinate lift, duration and cam position to manage residual gas, turbine energy and cylinder filling.

On exhaust-side applications, it selects the valve event that preserves exhaust-pulse energy and gas velocity at lower speed, helping the turbine respond sooner. At higher airflow, the larger, longer-duration profile reduces restriction. The ECM coordinates AVS with cam phasing, ignition, throttle and wastegate control; the benefit comes from the complete charge-management strategy.

Common complaints include a MIL or EPC lamp, rough operation, reduced power and valve-lift actuator codes. Depending on the application, technicians may encounter P11A1 through P11B8 electrical or implausible-signal faults. Likely causes include an open or shorted actuator coil, connector or harness damage, incorrect actuator-to-cam clearance, a sticking actuator pin, or a cam piece that cannot slide because of wear, damage or contamination.

Audi TSB 2031085/1 addresses implausible cam-actuator signals on 2009-2012 3.2 FSI applications. It calls for measuring actuator-pin clearance and specifies a revised actuator at 0.9 mm or greater; Audi also noted an optimized camshaft frame from July 2011.

When working on this, start diagnosis with a full scan, freeze-frame data and the appropriate output test or basic setting. Confirm power, ground and coil integrity before condemning the camshaft, and separate AVS codes from cam-phaser or oil-pressure faults.

The BMW N54 is known for its smooth power delivery, nearly nonexistent turbo lag and robust forged internals. It’s also known to suffer from a few common issues, one of which is its electric water pump. That’s right, the water pump, the component that circulates coolant throughout the engine cooling circuit, is electric.

The water pumps we’re discussing are used in a number of vehicles. This includes the 128i, 325i, 325xi, 330i, 330xi, 525i, 525xi, 528i, 528xi, 530i, 530xi, X3, X5, and Z4. Let’s take a closer look at this unique water pump, how to replace it efficiently and what other components should be replaced along with it.

Electric water pumps are becoming more and more common on modern engines. Electric auxiliary water pumps have been around for a long time. Their job is to circulate warm coolant through the heater core or to circulate coolant throughout an additional cooling circuit, such as a water-to-air charge air cooler.

The electric water pump on the N54 has a power output of 400W, and a maximum flow rate of 9,000 liters per hour. The motor power is electronically controlled by the control module inside the pump housing, and this module is connected via the communication BUS to the Digital Motor Electrics (DME), also known as the engine control unit or ECU. The DME uses the engine load, the operating mode and the data from the temperature sensors to calculate the required cooling output, then commands the electric pump according to the current operating conditions. The electric pump regulates its speed based on this command from the DME. Coolant flows through the motor inside the pump, providing cooling to both the motor and the electronic module.
The electric water pump circulates coolant even after the engine has been shut off. Doing this can cool down the turbochargers and help to prolong their service life.
Electric water pumps on the N54 have been known to fail around 60,000-80,000 miles.

When the DME detects an issue with the pump, or if it sees engine coolant temps rising, it will notify the driver through the instrument cluster. This may take the form of one of two different messages: “Engine Temp High – Drive Moderately” displayed in yellow, or “Engine Overheat – Stop” displayed in red. The vehicle may go into “limp mode” which limits the engine RPM and available gear selection in an effort to protect engine components from damage. The electric cooling fan will usually jump to its maximum speed. You may also find stored 2E81 and/or 2E82 trouble codes, which indicate a problem with the pump.
There are two other cooling system issues you should be on the lookout for whenever you’re inspecting or quoting a replacement to a customer: The coolant inlet pipe, and the “Mickey Mouse” hose.

The coolant inlet pipe is an aluminum pipe with a rubber elbow on one end and an aluminum flange on the other end. The aluminum flange bolts up to the cylinder head between the turbochargers, and the rubber elbow connects to the water pump. The aluminum portion of this component should last for a long, long time, but the rubber elbow is prone to failing. This is largely due to the fact that it is mounted so close to the front turbocharger.

All in all, it’ll take 6.7+ hours to replace this pipe, which feels like a waste if the rubber elbow is the only part that really failed. Thankfully, Rein offers the hose by itself, and it should take only an hour to install.

One of the many hoses which connects to the thermostat and water pump connects to the front of the engine just under the valve cover. This hose is commonly referred to as the “Mickey Mouse hose” due to the unique shape of the flange. This flange is made of plastic, and we all know how plastic parts can become brittle and crack after years of heat-cycling.

Just like the coolant inlet pipe, this flange is available only from BMW with the hose attached. Rein came up with a solution in the form of a metal replacement connector which can be purchased with or without the hose attached.

Through a joint venture with two other companies, Honda has developed underlaying technology for a magnetic-coupling wireless power transfer road system (WPT road system), which will enable wireless in-motion charging of EVs, according to a press release.
Honda R&D, Taisei Corp. (Taisei), and Taisei Rotec Corp. (Taisei Rotec) plan to conduct demonstration testing of the system beginning in the Japanese 2027 fiscal year.
The system combines proprietary technology from each of the companies:
- Taisei: High-response DC power supply system
- Taisei Rotec: Technology for embedding equipment in roads

“With these technologies, the system achieves high-power wireless power transfer (WPT) and excellent ease of installation in road pavement, envisioning applications for a wide range of mobility products, from passenger EVs to large commercial EVs,” the release states.

Honda says it has been working on dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT) technology since 2021. The technology supplies power to vehicles while they are in motion and reduces the frequency of charging needed at home or at a charging station, the release states.

“Initially, Honda will strive to put DWPT technology into practical use in the logistics and transportation sectors, where DWPT technology is expected to deliver significant benefits,” the release states.

Honda, Taisei, and Taisei Rotec have been conducting research and development of the magnetic-coupling WPT road system since 2025, according to the release. This has resulted in the development of the underlaying technology for the system.
- DC distribution-based ground assembly (GA) systems that connect multiple GA units embedded in the road using a DC connection
- A vehicle assembly (VA) unit installed on the vehicle

Honda says that to achieve the real-world implementation of a WPT road system, it is essential to develop GA units and pavement structures with sufficient strength to withstand the loads of large commercial vehicles and a power transfer system capable of handling high-power transfer to EVs driving at high speeds, while also offering excellent practicality for installation in roads.
Testing at the T-FIELD/SATTE focused on GA units and pavement structures capable of withstanding the traffic of large vehicles with a gross vehicle weight of about 20 tons.
It also tested whether the DC power supply systems can supply high-power electricity to a DC distribution-based GA system with high responsiveness and stability.
The GA units were also tested for highly practical installation and future upgrades.
“Through these tests, the three companies will strive to ensure both power transfer performance and the safety of the GA units as structures embedded in the roadway,” the release states.

After this phase, the companies plan to further verify performance at high power output levels of up to 150 kW for potential application to large commercial vehicles, as well as verification of the reliability of WPT performance for vehicles traveling at high speeds.

Honda says that all three companies will participate in the “Tateyama Project” starting during the Japanese 2027 fiscal year. It will include demonstration testing of DWPT technology conducted by East Nippon Expressway Company Limited on the Tateyama Expressway in Chiba, Japan.

“Striving to realize a sustainable mobility society where people can enjoy freedom of mobility well into the future, Honda will continue to pursue co-creation with a diverse range of partners beyond the automotive industry, including road infrastructure-related businesses, government agencies and energy-related businesses,” the release states.

U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-District 17) has filed a bill that would require auto dealerships and other resale channels selling used vehicles to sell them with functional airbag systems, or if an airbag is missing or disabled, to clearly disclose that.

If passed, the bill would mean up to life in prison for sellers if someone dies as a result of a vehicle sold at an auction or dealership without disclosing the vehicle is missing an airbag or is equipped with a disabled one.
Lawler filed the Anthony Amoros Law Right to Know Act this week, according to a press release from his office.

Anthony Amoros died in 2013 at the age of 18 after crashing his car on a windy stretch of road, according to a New York CBS News report. Amoros’s family purchased the vehicle without knowing it lacked an airbag.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill titled “Anthony Amoros Law” in 2021 that prohibits used car dealers from selling vehicles without a working airbag, according to Spectrum News. The law requires sellers to provide consumers with certification that the vehicle is equipped with an airbag.

“Every driver and passenger deserves to know that the vehicle they are getting into is safe, and this bill will help protect consumers by making sure they have the information they need to make informed decisions,” Lawler said in his press release. “This legislation will ensure dealerships and third-party sellers cannot sell these vehicles without clearly informing consumers of the safety risks.”
Lawler’s bill would require sellers to disclose that vehicles don’t have a working airbag on the front of the sales contract receipt and invoice.
The proposed law would give state officials or agencies authority to regulate and enforce compliance after Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice.
The FTC will have the right to intervene in any action or file a petition of appeal.
Penalties outlined in the bill allow for a court to award an additional $25,000 for an action that involves death or paralysis.
The bill states that those who knowingly sell a vehicle without a working airbag and disclosure could be fined and face up to 10 years in prison.
It adds that a seller could face up to 20 years in prison if someone is seriously injured, including paralysis.
The bill also defines a “deficiency” as a vehicle without a functional airbag system and/or inflatable restraint system.

Counterfeit airbags are not specifically mentioned in the bill. However, it’s likely that vehicles without an airbag or a deficient airbag system travel through the same salvage routes as vehicles with counterfeit airbags.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently identified an 11th death caused by a counterfeit airbag part that the agency banned earlier this year.
The death happened Aug. 27 in Dallas, Texas, and is described as an otherwise survivable crash by NHTSA.

Teena Bohi, an Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council (A2C2) board member, said during a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) meeting in July that NHTSA’s investigation has uncovered how dangerous counterfeit parts find their way into vehicles.

“The totaling of a vehicle isn’t a cut-and-dried process,” Bohi says. “The value is driven depending on whether it is self-insured, the state the vehicle was in, the insurer’s own practices, processes, and thresholds. There is a lot that goes into just determining if the vehicle is totaled.”

Next, the vehicle often goes to an auction. If it is a public auction, an airbag deployment will possibly be reported to the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System (NMVTIS). The system is a database meant to prevent the resale of stolen vehicles and track unsafe salvage cars. If the vehicle goes to a wholesale or private auction, the previous crash information is not always captured, she said.

According to an Automotive News opinion piece, about 2.5 million vehicles were totaled by insurers last year before eventually returning to U.S. roadways. It says that a shift in insurers totaling more vehicles, along with the higher cost of new and used vehicles, has forced more dealers to repair and sell salvaged-titled vehicles.
Copart CEO Jeff Liaw discussed how salvaging a car for auction competes with collision repairs during a 2025 earnings call.

“Even an insurance carrier can sell their cars through other intermediaries; they can have more of them repaired,” Liaw said in the September call. “In many respects, we compete with the repair shops. The higher the returns we generate, the more we can win the rights to resolve that claim versus the repair industry. The lower the returns we generate, the more we lose head-to-head against the repair shops as well. There are a number of competitive threats that we face on any given day.”
He went on to describe how delivering “excellent service,” such as expediting cycle times and interacting with policyholders, can drive auction returns.
Those vehicles eventually have to be rebuilt before returning to the road — a process Bohi said can create opportunities for counterfeit safety components to enter the supply chain.
After repairs, vehicles are retitled, and the process can vary state to state, including the inspection process, Bohi says. Many don’t require airbag inspections.
“There are a lot of gaps where attention could be focused that could help address these types of issues,” Bohi said.
The Automotive News piece suggests that state processes, including inspection requirements, may need reworking as the market shifts to more dealers selling salvaged titles.
